Learning to Draw ASCII Improves Spatial Reasoning in Language Models

Shiyuan Huang ††thanks: Equal Contribution    Li Liu11footnotemark: 1    Jincheng He    Leilani H. Gilpin ††thanks: Corresponding Author: lgilpin@ucsc.edu Affiliation: University of California, Santa Cruz Affiliation: {shuan101, lliu112, jhe516, lgilpin}@ucsc.edu
Abstract

When faced with complex spatial problems, humans naturally sketch layouts to organize their thinking, and the act of drawing further sharpens their understanding. In this work, we ask whether a similar principle holds for Large Language Models (LLMs): can learning to construct explicit visual layouts from spatial descriptions instill genuine spatial understanding? We introduce Text2Space, a dataset that pairs natural language descriptions with ground-truth ASCII grid layouts and spatial QA pairs, enabling us to separate failures in constructing spatial representations from failures in reasoning over them. We adopt ASCII because it is human-readable, operates entirely within the token space of language models, and encodes spatial relations in a structurally verifiable form. Our evaluation reveals a pronounced “Read-Write Asymmetry”: LLMs interpret ASCII representations effectively but struggle to produce them from text, and these construction errors propagate to incorrect answers downstream. To address this limitation, we train models on layout construction (Text→\rightarrowASCII) and find that it significantly improves spatial reasoning from text alone, even without producing any ASCII at inference time. Combining construction with comprehension training further amplifies these gains. Crucially, these improvements transfer to three external spatial reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating that, much as sketching sharpens human spatial thinking, learning to construct explicit layouts instills spatial understanding that generalizes beyond the training format.

1 Introduction

Spatial reasoning (Byrne and Johnson-Laird, 1989; Newcombe and Huttenlocher, 2000) is fundamental to human cognition (Malanchini et al., 2020). As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to complex spatial reasoning tasks, a growing body of work has emerged to evaluate their capabilities in this domain (Li et al., 2024; Cohn and Hernandez-Orallo, 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2024).

However, existing benchmarks are limited to evaluating final answers (Yamada et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023). When a model fails, it is unclear whether the error stems from a flawed spatial representation or from faulty reasoning over a correct one. More critically, even correct answers may reflect surface-level pattern matching rather than robust spatial understanding. A model can exploit lexical cues in simple configurations yet fail unpredictably as spatial complexity grows. Prior work on faithful reasoning has shown that correct answers produced through unreliable intermediate steps offer no guarantee of consistent behavior on novel problems (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020; Creswell and Shanahan, 2022; Parcalabescu and Frank, 2024; Xiong et al., 2025). Without a way to verify the model’s intermediate spatial representation, these failure modes remain invisible.

To open this black box, we use ASCII grid layouts as an explicit, structured text that makes the reasoning process itself observable. The ASCII representation is well suited as this diagnostic lens because it lives within the model’s own token space, is immediately interpretable by humans, and can be formally verified against ground truth. We introduce Text2Space, a benchmark of diverse spatial configurations paired with natural language descriptions, images, and three styles of ASCII grids. Each instance includes a ground-truth layout, providing verifiable supervision for both diagnosing representation failures and training models toward robust spatial understanding.

Figure 1 outlines our study design, which explores two processes between natural language and ASCII: construction turns text into layouts, and comprehension reads spatial relations from them. Using Text2Space, we contribute three investigations. First, we benchmark language models on ASCII comprehension, generation, and reasoning. Second, we examine the reasoning process by assessing whether ASCII representations faithfully support model reasoning. Most importantly, we investigate whether the spatial understanding acquired through ASCII-based learning generalizes to purely linguistic spatial reasoning tasks.

Our evaluation yields three principal findings that progressively identify a representation bottleneck (what we call the construction gap) and show how to mitigate it. Finding 1: Models can understand spatial layouts but struggle to generate them. Across all models, comprehending ASCII diagrams is substantially easier than constructing them from text, identifying construction as the primary constraint. Finding 2: This construction gap directly harms reasoning. When models sketch layouts as an intermediate step, their construction errors propagate to the final answer. Yet when accurate ASCII is provided instead, reasoning improves substantially over text alone, showing that the bottleneck is not reasoning itself but the quality of the representation it operates over. Finding 3: Training on building construction reduces the asymmetry and the benefits generalize. Training models on layout construction improves spatial reasoning from text alone, even without producing any ASCII at inference time. Comprehension training alone does not consistently improve performance, but it leads to gains when combined with construction, producing the strongest overall results. These gains transfer to three external benchmarks, confirming that construction training builds transferable spatial understanding rather than format-specific heuristics.

We present three contributions: (1) a benchmark of spatial configurations paired with ground-truth ASCII layouts, enabling evaluation that separates representation failures from reasoning failures; (2) identification of the construction gap, showing that models comprehend spatial layouts more reliably than they construct them and that this asymmetry propagates into downstream reasoning; and (3) empirical evidence that learning to construct spatial layouts fosters transferable internal spatial understanding, validated on three external benchmarks.

2 Related Work

Linguistic Spatial Reasoning Benchmarks.

Early work on spatial language processing focused on extracting formal representations from natural language text (Kordjamshidi et al., 2011). Subsequent benchmarks like bAbI (Weston et al., 2015) introduced positional reasoning, while StepGame (Shi et al., 2022) and SpartQA (Mirzaee et al., 2021) advanced the field with more complicated reasoning and broader linguistic coverage. However, a critical limitation remains across these benchmarks: they rely exclusively on final-answer accuracy. This "black-box" evaluation obscures the underlying inference process, making it impossible to distinguish between failures in representation and failures in reasoning. Our work addresses this methodological gap by introducing ground-truth intermediate representations, enabling precise diagnosis of spatial reasoning errors.

While integrating visual modalities (VLMs) offers a potential remedy for spatial understanding, recent studies reveal that VLMs face their own challenges in visual perception (Liu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024; Kamath et al., 2023) and spatial reasoning (Chen et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a; Ogezi and Shi, 2025). Rather than relying on a separate visual encoder, we use ASCII grids to represent spatial layouts entirely within the language model’s native token space. These text-native grids serve a dual purpose: they act not only as a reasoning source within the context but also as a verifiable representation of all spatial relations.

ASCII and Spatial Representation.

The utility of intermediate reasoning steps is well-established through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting (Wei et al., 2022) and its extensions, such as Tree-of-Thoughts (Yao et al., 2023) and latent reasoning (Hao et al., 2024). Beyond purely linguistic traces, prior work has shown that symbolic, text-native spatial representations can effectively support spatial reasoning in language models, including grid-based worlds and discrete relational layouts (Côté et al., 2018). Visualization-of-Thought (Wu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025) draws on human mental imagery to generate symbolic or pixel-level visualizations for spatial reasoning. While we share the intuition that explicit spatial construction aids reasoning, we focus on a different question: when and why does this process fail, and can training on it improve performance? We use ASCII as a diagnostic medium because, unlike natural language, its spatial outputs are structurally verifiable against ground truth.

Generalization of Spatial Reasoning.

Recent research demonstrates that enhancing specific capabilities in LLMs often yields transfer benefits to other domains. For instance, Shao et al. (2024) indicate that training on mathematics improves general reasoning benchmarks, not just quantitative tasks. Prior work shows that spatial training benefits visual reasoning tasks (Wei et al., 2025; Han et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025), typically through training on perception or comprehension objectives. We study a complementary mechanism: whether learning to construct spatial layouts can strengthen spatial understanding in language models, yielding transferable gains in spatial reasoning.

3 Text2Space Dataset

We introduce Text2Space, a dataset pairing each natural language description with a ground-truth ASCII layout, a rendered image, and a query-answer pair, all derived from one spatial graph. The layout serves as a verifiable reference for construction, comprehension, and downstream reasoning. Figure 2 shows an example.

3.1 Data Generation

The dataset is constructed from connected spatial graphs where entities are linked via eight directional relationships: above, below, left, right, upper-left, upper-right, lower-left, lower-right. All relations adhere to a unified coordinate system, serving as the ground truth for both ASCII diagrams and rendered images. Instances are generated using a breadth-first search (BFS) procedure to guarantee connectivity. We enforce strict validation rules: self-loops and duplicate edges are prohibited, and any configuration conflicting with existing spatial constraints is rejected. These safeguards ensure every instance represents a valid, internally consistent topology. A detailed data generation process is presented in the Appendix F.

We vary complexity from simple two-component structures to intricate graphs with up to eight components and twelve relations, capturing configurations that require transitive reasoning across multiple inference steps. Each instance includes natural language descriptions synthesized from the spatial graph, using diverse synonyms to ensure linguistic variation. Corresponding queries are designed so that target object pairs admit unique inferability, guaranteeing a single unambiguous spatial relation.

3.2 Multi-Format Representations

ASCII Visualization: We include three rendering styles to test robustness against formatting variations. The simple format uses minimal spacing without borders for clarity. The grid format introduces structure using +, -, and | characters. The panel format employs box-drawing characters for a visually distinct layout. Image Representation: The spatial arrangement is also rendered in a standardized image format with configurable grid lines and directional arrows, serving as both a multimodal evaluation target and a human-readable reference. Further dataset details and data examples are provided in Appendix A.

4 Experiments

We split Text2Space into training and test sets, with the test set consisting of 1,000 samples used in the following experiments. We choose the ASCII grid format throughout our experiments; details of this format are provided in Appendix B. Our experiments address three questions in sequence. Benchmarking: Can models both read and draw spatial layouts, and where does the gap lie? Reasoning process: When models sketch a layout as an intermediate step, does the quality of that sketch help or hurt downstream reasoning? Generalization: Does training on layout construction instill spatial understanding that transfers to text-only reasoning and external benchmarks, even when no layout is produced at inference time?

4.1 Models

We evaluate two model categories. Instruct models: including Llama-3-70B-Instruct (AI@Meta, 2024), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024; Team, 2024), Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 (Team, 2025), GPT-4.1 (OpenAI, 2025a). Thinking model: gpt-oss-20B (OpenAI, 2025b). Unless otherwise specified, we use default settings and apply 5-shot prompting (Brown et al., 2020) to ensure consistency.

4.2 Task Setups

Since ASCII is a unique representation that encodes two-dimensional spatial structure within a one-dimensional token sequence, we first evaluate language models’ ability to understand and generate ASCII representations. Specifically, we assess two complementary capabilities: generating an ASCII representation from a textual description (Desc→\rightarrowASCII) and generating a natural-language description from an ASCII representation (ASCII→\rightarrowDesc).

We then evaluate spatial reasoning tasks, denoted ℛ\mathcal{R}, in which the model is given a reasoning source and asked to answer queries about spatial relationships. ℛDesc\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc}} refers to reasoning from textual descriptions alone, while ℛASCII\mathcal{R}_{\text{ASCII}} refers to reasoning from ASCII representations alone. Beyond reasoning from a single source, we investigate the role of ASCII as an intermediate step alongside descriptions through two generation orders. In ℛDesc:(Ans, ASCII)\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc:(Ans, ASCII)}}, the model first produces the answer and then generates an ASCII representation. In ℛDesc:(ASCII, Ans)\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc:(ASCII, Ans)}}, the model first generates an ASCII representation and then uses it to answer the query. For both orders, we consider one-turn generation, where the model produces both outputs within a single response, and two-turn generation, where the second output is elicited via a follow-up prompt. The two generation orders mirror established self-explanation paradigms (Huang et al., 2023; Madsen et al., 2024): we compare two generation orders: predict-then-explain versus explain-then-predict (Camburu et al., 2018).

Finally, we evaluate ℛDesc+ASCII\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc+ASCII}}. In this phase, we substitute the model-generated ASCII with the ground-truth ASCII before the model answers the query. This replacement strategy simulates an ideal reasoning process, allowing us to assess the upper-bound performance of the model when guided by an ideal spatial representation.

4.3 Evaluation Methods

Our evaluation protocol targets three key aspects of the model’s performance: QA Correctness: For the spatial reasoning QA tasks, we validate the prediction against a predefined set of relation aliases. Representation Alignment: For the ASCII↔\leftrightarrowDesc conversion tasks, we measure the correspondence between converted representations. For ASCII→\rightarrowDesc, the ASCII diagram is treated as the reference. We evaluate, across all generated descriptions, the percentage that can be correctly inferred from the given ASCII representation. For Desc→\rightarrowASCII, we evaluate the generated ASCII diagrams, ℛDesc:(Ans, ASCII)\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc:(Ans, ASCII)}} and ℛDesc:(ASCII, Ans)\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc:(ASCII, Ans)}}, by taking the description as the reference and measuring the proportion of the description that is correctly reflected in the ASCII output. Reasoning Consistency: For the joint generation settings, we introduce two complementary metrics to analyze internal coherence. Consistency(Cons): Measures the alignment between the generated ASCII and the generated Answer. This determines if the model’s intermediate output supports its final prediction. Consistency Accuracy(C_Acc): Measures answer accuracy strictly on instances where the ASCII and Answer are consistent. By controlling for internal coherence, this isolates the model’s reasoning capability, helping distinguish whether errors arise from failures in constructing spatial representations or from limitations in reasoning over them.

4.4 Learning Spatial Relations with ASCII

We propose that ASCII layouts function as a structured reasoning intermediate: a verifiable “cognitive map” that makes spatial relationships explicit. We hypothesize that learning to construct such maps (Lightman et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025b) consolidates spatial logic during training. If so, models trained on layout construction should improve on spatial reasoning tasks even without producing any layout at inference time, and the benefit should transfer beyond the training format. To test and disentangle the understanding and generation of ASCII representations, we design three configurations. Learning to Construct (Desc→\rightarrowASCII) forces the model to actively construct spatial layouts from text (performing “mental mapping”). Learning to Comprehend (ASCII→\rightarrowDesc) focuses on parsing and verbalizing ASCII representations. Bidirectional Alignment (Desc↔\leftrightarrowASCII) combines both tasks simultaneously.

We fine-tuned Qwen3-30B-A3B on 4x NVIDIA A40 GPUs using the SFTTrainer from the HuggingFace TRL library (von Werra et al., 2020). We employed Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2021; Mangrulkar et al., 2022) for parameter-efficient training, utilizing a split of 4,000 training and 500 validation examples. We adhered to the default library configurations for all other settings; full training details are provided in Appendix C.

We evaluate performance on the Spatial Reasoning Task (ℛDesc\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc}}), where models answer spatial relations solely from natural language descriptions without explicit ASCII input. To assess whether the benefits extend beyond our benchmark, we further evaluate on three external tasks that each target a different facet of spatial cognition: StepGame (Shi et al., 2022; Rizvi et al., 2024) examines compositional directional navigation, bAbI task 19 (Weston et al., 2015) tests route planning through connected locations, and SpartQA (Mirzaee et al., 2021) challenges models with complex spatial questions in rich natural language. None of these tasks involve ASCII, and we evaluate the model’s performance with zero-shot prompting setting. If construction training instills generalizable spatial understanding, gains should appear on these tasks despite the format mismatch.

5 Results and Discussion

5.1 Benchmarking

ASCII Understanding and Generation

Table 1 presents the results for the Desc↔\leftrightarrowASCII conversion tasks. Across all models, we observe a clear and consistent asymmetry: interpretation (ASCII→\rightarrowDesc) significantly outperforms generation (Desc→\rightarrowASCII). This pattern suggests that while models are relatively proficient at “reading” or identifying patterns in ASCII, they struggle significantly more with “drawing” it correctly. Even the reasoning model gpt-oss-20B fails to construct accurate layouts in 56% of cases, despite robust interpretative success.

The disparity spans 13 to 27 percentage points across all evaluated models (Table 1), pointing to a systematic bottleneck rather than an incidental failure mode. Interpretation relies on local pattern recognition within a provided grid, whereas generation demands global constraint satisfaction, jointly positioning all entities so that every described relation is upheld. The construction bottleneck matters not as a standalone finding but because of its downstream consequences. As we show next, this construction deficit directly propagates to reasoning failures, and mitigating it through targeted training leads to spatial understanding that transfers beyond the ASCII format (Section 5.3).

Spatial Reasoning Performance

Table 2 reports accuracy on spatial reasoning tasks (ℛ\mathcal{R}) under different settings. On the text-only baseline (ℛDesc\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc}}), accuracy ranges from 42.0% (Qwen2.5-7B) to 93.3% (gpt-oss-20B). This spread confirms that our benchmark meaningfully differentiates spatial reasoning ability, yet most models have substantial room to improve. This motivates examining whether ASCII representations can deepen spatial understanding and narrow this gap.

Providing ASCII as input substantially refines performance. Most models reason more accurately from ASCII alone (ℛASCII\mathcal{R}_{\text{ASCII}}) than from text descriptions (ℛDesc\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc}}), and the combination of both (ℛDesc+ASCII\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc+ASCII}}) yields the highest accuracy. This shows that ASCII serves as a critical signal for resolving spatial ambiguities in natural language.

In contrast, model-generated ASCII as an intermediate step before answering does not improve reasoning. Answering first and then drawing (ℛDesc(Ans, ASCII)\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc(Ans, ASCII)}}) roughly matches the text-only baseline (ℛDesc\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc}}), while drawing first and then answering (ℛDesc(ASCII, Ans)\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc(ASCII, Ans)}}) drops below it across all base models in both one-turn and two-turn settings. With generated ASCII accuracy at only 12-50% across models, the sketches are not accurate enough to serve as a promising reasoning scaffold. Since provided ASCII yields the highest accuracy while model-generated ASCII degrades it, the bottleneck is sketch quality, not the format itself. This echoes prior findings that generating intermediate artifacts can reduce task accuracy (Camburu et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2023). However, unlike unstructured self-explanations or textual CoT (Wei et al., 2022), where intermediate errors are difficult to detect, ASCII is structurally verifiable. This allows us to directly trace the degradation to flawed construction rather than treating it as a black-box effect. Models can reason over spatial layouts when provided, but cannot yet produce them reliably enough to support their own reasoning.

This diagnosis points to a concrete path forward: since the deficiency lies in representation construction, the next step is to examine whether training on this capability can strengthen the model’s spatial understanding. We first analyze whether the model’s generated layouts are internally coherent with its answers, using consistency as an unsupervised signal of reasoning reliability (Section 5.2). We then investigate whether training on layout construction can instill the spatial understanding needed to bridge this discrepancy (Section 5.3).

5.2 Consistency Analysis in Spatial Reasoning

Table 3 shows the alignment between ASCII representations and textual answers across both output orders and turn settings. We report three key metrics: (1) Answer Accuracy measures overall task performance; (2) Consistency quantifies the alignment between the generated ASCII and the textual answer; and (3) Consistent Accuracy evaluates correctness specifically on instances where the representation and answer correspond.

In the one-turn generation setting, producing the ASCII representation before the answer does not improve consistency. Similar consistency across output orders suggests that the model does not clearly use the ASCII as a reasoning scaffold, with both outputs likely reflecting the same underlying representation. In the two-turn generation setting, we observed an improved consistency rate, where the model first generates either the answer or the ASCII, and is then prompted to produce the other. The consistency gap between ℛDesc:(Ans, ASCII)\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc:(Ans, ASCII)}} and ℛDesc:(ASCII, Ans)\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc:(ASCII, Ans)}} indicates that the response to the follow-up query is strongly influenced by the previously generated output. Despite this notable improvement in consistency, answer accuracy increases only marginally. This limited gain may partly reflect to the suboptimal quality of the generated ASCII representations, which correlates with lower answer accuracy (Table 2).

Nevertheless, consistency remains a valuable indicator, particularly as it requires no ground-truth annotations for either layout or the answer. While prior work has applied Natural Language Inference (NLI) to assess reasoning via consistency (Wang et al., 2022; Lyu et al., 2023; Kumar and Talukdar, 2020), our approach benefits from the explicit verifiability of the generated artifact. Unlike unstructured text, ASCII representations enforce strict spatial constraints and encode the full spatial configuration, not just the queried pair, allowing us to objectively assess the alignment between the representation and the answer. We observe that when the model’s ASCII representation and its textual answer agree, the answer is far more likely to be correct. This consistency check requires no ground-truth labels: the ASCII itself is structurally verifiable, so agreement between the two outputs serves as an unsupervised reliability signal.

Our results show “ASCII as a Verifier” as a promising direction. The structural constraints imposed by ASCII suggest that cross-representation consistency may provide a more reliable signal of reasoning validity than text-only self-consistency. Future work may explore integrating such structured verification signals into reasoning pipelines, both as an error-detection mechanism and as a guiding objective for improving intermediate representation construction.

5.3 Learning Spatial Relations with ASCII

Table 1 details the performance on conversion tasks after fine-tuning. We note that construction training is an auxiliary task: the model learns to produce ASCII layouts, not to answer spatial questions. Construction training (FTD→A{}_{\text{D}\rightarrow\text{A}}) raises generation accuracy (Desc→\rightarrowASCII) from 29.2% to 67.9%, a much larger gain than comprehension training achieves (Desc←\leftarrowASCII: 55.8% to 66.5%). The disparity confirms that ASCII generation is the primary bottleneck, with far more room for improvement. Unidirectional training improves the targeted direction but slightly degrades the other, while joint training (Desc↔\leftrightarrowASCII) improves both tasks (64.6% generation, 68.4% understanding) without this trade-off.

We now evaluate whether these improvements transfer to the downstream spatial reasoning task (ℛDesc\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc}}), which does not generate ASCII at inference time but requires answering spatial queries from text alone, a task format entirely absent from fine-tuning. Table 2 shows that construction training (FTD→A{}_{\text{D}\rightarrow\text{A}}) improves accuracy by over 7 percentage points, indicating that learning to construct spatial layouts strengthens spatial reasoning from text alone. In contrast, comprehension training (FTD←A{}_{\text{D}\leftarrow\text{A}}) fails to improve performance and falls slightly below the baseline, suggesting that improved comprehension without a reliable spatial representation as its foundation is not just insufficient but counterproductive. Since both conditions expose the model to identical spatial configurations, the divergence isolates construction as the active ingredient, not mere exposure to spatial data.

Fine-tuning on layout construction substantially improves ASCII accuracy for ℛDesc:(Ans, ASCII)\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc:(Ans, ASCII)}} and ℛDesc:(ASCII, Ans)\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc:(ASCII, Ans)}}, reversing the pattern from Section 5.1: accurate sketches now scaffold reasoning rather than mislead. The bottleneck was not the representation format but sketch quality: even after fine-tuning, ground-truth ASCII (ℛDesc+ASCII\mathcal{R}_{\text{Desc+ASCII}}) still outperforms model-generated sketches, confirming that further improvements in construction will yield additional reasoning gains.

The persistent advantage of externally provided layouts, even after construction training, parallels human spatial cognition. In a preliminary human validation (Appendix I), participants achieve substantially higher accuracy with access to ASCII layouts than with text descriptions alone. Mentally reconstructing spatial structure from sequential text is inherently more demanding than reading a provided layout for both humans and models.

The consistency analysis (Table 3) tells a complementary story. Construction training improves consistency between the model’s sketch and its answer far more than comprehension training does. The mechanism is intuitive: when the sketch is accurate, it reinforces the textual answer; when it remains flawed, better comprehension only makes the model more aware of the conflict between its noisy sketch and the description. Construction training thus both improves consistency and ensures that consistent instances are more likely to be correct. The confusion matrices (Appendix, Figure 4) corroborate this: construction training reduces confusions between spatially adjacent directions, sharpening directional boundaries.

Table 4 tests whether these gains extend beyond Text2Space by evaluating on three external benchmarks under zero-shot prompting, without ASCII at inference time. Both configurations that include construction training (FTD→A{}_{\text{D}\rightarrow\text{A}} and FTD↔A{}_{\text{D}\leftrightarrow\text{A}}) improve on all three benchmarks, while comprehension training alone does not, confirming construction as the necessary ingredient for transfer. Bidirectional training further improves over construction alone on two of three benchmarks, with 3.6 percentage points on bAbI task 19 and 5.7 percentage points on SpartQA, showing that comprehension further strengthens the foundations of spatial cognition that construction provides. Comprehension training (FTD←A{}_{\text{D}\leftarrow\text{A}}) on its own shows an inconsistent pattern: it degrades StepGame, which tests precise directional navigation, yet yields large gains on SpartQA, which emphasizes parsing complex spatial language. This aligns with each task’s demands and shows that comprehension alone cannot substitute for construction.

6 Conclusion

We investigate whether training language models to construct explicit spatial layouts can instill genuine spatial understanding. Using ASCII grids as a diagnostic instrument that is text-native, human-readable, and structurally verifiable, we introduce Text2Space, a benchmark to separate construction failures from reasoning failures.

Our results reveal a clear read-write asymmetry. Models can interpret spatial layouts effectively but struggle to construct them from text, and these construction errors propagate to downstream reasoning. Consistency analysis further shows that when a model’s ASCII representation agrees with its textual answer, answer accuracy is substantially higher. This agreement serves as an unsupervised reliability signal. Training models to construct layouts addresses this bottleneck directly: spatial reasoning from text improves even without active sketching at inference time, and the benefit transfers to three external benchmarks (StepGame, bAbI, SpartQA) that require spatial understanding. Only configurations that include construction training generalize across all three benchmarks, with the combination of construction and comprehension yielding the strongest gains. These results indicate that the spatial understanding gained through layout construction is not format-specific but foundational, enabling models to reason more effectively across diverse task formulations.

Limitations

ASCII grids are one instantiation of our approach, chosen for diagnostic precision and structural verifiability. This scope entails several boundaries: we do not explore alternative formats such as coordinate lists or scene graphs, nor spatial problems involving continuous geometry, pixel-level perception, or 3D environments. As a discrete abstraction, ASCII does not capture the richness of continuous spatial perception, and our synthetic benchmark may not fully represent real-world noise and ambiguity. Future work could examine whether construction training transfers to other model families and whether richer formats scale to more complex spatial environments.

Our evaluation relies on answer accuracy and consistency between generated diagrams and predictions. These metrics provide observable, verifiable signals of reasoning behavior but do not directly reveal the model’s internal representations. While ASCII’s structure offers a foundation for iterative verification and self-correction, this work does not explore such mechanisms.

Appendix

Appendix A Dataset Details

Table 5 shows possible values for each field in Text2Space. The dataset is in English, covering various terminologies including cardinal directions (e.g., ‘North’), clock-face references (e.g., ‘3 o’clock’), and standard spatial prepositions (e.g., ‘left of’). Figure 3 and Table  8 provides data statistics for the full dataset and test set.

Appendix B ASCII Format Choice

Using three different ASCII representations as input, we conduct two experiments to determine the most suitable format. The first experiment evaluates the interpretation of natural language descriptions from ASCII (ASCII →\rightarrow Desc), while the second assesses spatial reasoning directly from ASCII (ℛASCII\mathcal{R}_{\text{ASCII}}). As shown in Table 6, performance on ASCII →\rightarrow Desc is comparable across all three formats. In contrast, for ℛASCII\mathcal{R}_{\text{ASCII}}, the grid-based representation yields substantially higher performance. Accordingly, we adopt the grid format in all subsequent experiments.

Appendix C Training configurations

Appendix D Confusion matrices for spatial reasoning predictions

Figure 4 presents the confusion matrices for spatial reasoning predictions before and after fine-tuning on the ASCII–description conversion tasks. Fine-tuning results in stronger concentration along the diagonal and reduces systematic confusions between spatially related classes, indicating improved internal organization of spatial representations rather than uniform scaling of prediction confidence.

Appendix E F1 Scores

Table 9 reports the F1 scores for spatial reasoning tasks. In line with Table 2, reasoning from ASCII alone generally outperforms reasoning from descriptions alone. While generating ASCII before answering hurts performance without fine-tuning, fine-tuning with explicit ASCII generation, either unidirectional (Desc→\rightarrowASCII) or bidirectional (Desc↔\leftrightarrowASCII), consistently improves performance when only descriptions are available at inference time.

Appendix I Human Validation

Human Validation Setup.

To quantify the impact of different input formats on spatial reasoning accuracy, we conducted a controlled human validation study with 11 evaluators divided into two groups: Team A (n=7n=7) and Team B (n=4n=4). We curated three distinct problem sets (Set X, Set Y, and Set Z), each containing 10 spatially complex examples. The design details are shown in Table 10

The study utilized a counterbalanced within-subjects design to disentangle the effect of input format from question difficulty. All participants completed three sessions:

  1. 1.

    Session 2 (Visual Baseline): Both teams evaluated Set Z using the ASCII-only format. Performance was highly consistent across groups (Team A: 0.986, Team B: 0.950), confirming that both teams possessed comparable visual reasoning baselines.

  2. 2.

    Sessions 1 & 3 (Crossover): We swapped the assignment of problem sets and formats between teams. Team A solved Set X using Description-only (Session 1) and Set Y using Description+ASCII (Session 3). Conversely, Team B solved Set Y using Description-only (Session 1) and Set X using Description+ASCII (Session 3).

This cross-over design ensures that Sets X and Y were evaluated in both text-only and combined formats, allowing for a direct comparison of performance on semantically identical questions.

Validation Results

Table 11 shows the substantial improvement achieved when reasoning from an ASCII-augmented description compared to reasoning from the description alone.

Appendix J Prompts and Outputs

J.1 Task Description →\rightarrow ASCII

⬇
---------
SYSTEM
---------
Assume you have expertise in spatial reasoning. Your task is to answer the following question to the best of your knowledge.
You will receive a scene description.
Your job is to generate the requested ASCII visualization and return the result as a compact JSON object.
Description -> ASCII Diagram.
Read the textual scene description and render the requested ASCII layout.
- Treat the canvas like a map: the first printed row is the top, and the last row is the bottom.
- The first column is the left edge; the last column is the right edge.
- Above = higher row; below = lower row (do not invert the vertical axis).
- Left = smaller column index; right = larger column index (do not mirror horizontally).
Formats:
- grid: <grid using + - | for borders>
Rendering & Positioning Rules
Use given uppercase letters (A, B, C, ...); don’t invent new ones.
Grid size is flexible - expand rows/cols as needed to fit all points.
Place all letters; if two overlap, stack them (e.g., "AF").
Relations are first -> second (e.g., "D to F" means D relative to F).
Positioning:
above/below -> same column
left/right -> same level
diagonals (upper/lower-left/right) -> one cell diagonally.
Keep perfect alignment for cardinal directions.
Adjacent items occupy neighboring cells; no diagonal drift.
Maintain uniform cell sizes and consistent borders.
Keep row alignment when depicting left/right relations; do not shift labels vertically.
Keep column alignment when depicting above/below relations; do not shift labels horizontally.
For diagonal relations, ensure the two entities occupy different rows and different columns.
Avoid inconsistent cell widths and do not introduce extra or missing letters.
Additional ASCII Guidance:
- Label every entity exactly as named in the description.
Input Notes:
- Use only the provided description to infer entity positions.
- Do not invent additional entities or relations when information is missing.
Output Notes:
- Produce ASCII views that faithfully match the described scene.
OUTPUT SCHEMA (JSON):
{
"ascii": {
"grid": "<grid using + - | for borders>"
}
}
Return ONLY a compact JSON object.
Do not include markdown fences or any extra text.
---------
USER
---------
Description:
B is to the lower-right of A. D is to the right of B. C is at the bottom-right of A. C is located below B.
---------
ASSISTANT
---------
{"ascii":{"grid":"+--+--+--+\n|A | | |\n+--+--+--+\n| |B |D |\n+--+--+--+\n| |C | |\n+--+--+--+"}}

⬇
---------
SYSTEM
---------
Assume you have expertise in spatial reasoning. Your task is to answer the following question to the best of your knowledge.

ASCII Diagram -> Description.

- The first column is the left edge; the last column is the right edge.
- Above = higher row; below = lower row (do not invert the vertical axis).

- Keep the description short and factual; avoid speculative language.
- The spatial summary will consist of sentences in the format "A is [relation] B." Each sentence should describe the relationship between exactly two objects.

}
